unit.title: Commodities
unit.description: Gold, oil, metals and agricultural commodities: what moves them and how to invest in them

texts: 25 years of gold
August 2000: you put **€1,000** into gold. Live through 25 years month by month, with **real data**, and decide whether to sell.
Gold hit a high in August 2011. How long did it take to beat it again?
A few months
About 2 years
Almost 9 years
It closed August 2011 at $1,829 and fell to $1,060 by the end of 2015 (**−42 %**). It didn't beat that high again until July 2020.
Make it to the end, whether you sell or not.
Anyone who held on multiplied their money more than 15 times, with **almost 9 years** below the 2011 high. Gold pays nothing: you only make money if someone pays more tomorrow.
You've sold. See what happens next…
More than 15 times over in 25 years, with a long slump in the middle.
Six times more! Will it keep rising non-stop?
It's already doubled. And it hasn't paid you a single euro of interest.
Hit «Start»: 25 years of gold, month by month
A little gold in the portfolio
January 2007: **€10,000** in US shares, rebalancing every year (real data up to 2025). Add some gold and look at the worst fall.
US shares (S&P 500)
Gold
Commodity basket
In the 2008 crisis, while shares were crashing, what did gold do?
It crashed just like shares
It rose while the stock market fell
It doubled
From October 2007 to February 2009, shares fell 51 % and gold rose 18 %.
With at least 10 % in gold, keep the worst fall from going past −40 %.

Because it sometimes rises when the stock market falls, **a little gold softened the worst fall**: from −51 % to −40 % with 20 %. But on its own, gold also fell as much as 43 %. And not every commodity is a safe haven: the broad basket fell 75 % and gained barely 15 % in 19 years.
That's a lot of gold: remember it pays no interest or dividends.
Look how the worst fall gets softer!
Raise gold bit by bit and look at the worst fall

steps.title: Why people buy gold
steps.body:
Gold **pays no interest or dividends**. People buy it as a **safe haven**: in a crisis, against inflation or when they don't trust currencies, and central banks stockpile it as a reserve. When **real interest rates** (after inflation) rise, holding it «costs» more and it tends to suffer.

Its 1980 high, about $850 an ounce, wasn't beaten until **2008**, and along the way it lost a lot of real value. In 2020 it passed $2,000 and in 2025, for the first time, **$4,000**.
steps.key: Gold sometimes protects you, but it doesn't produce anything.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for gold and see how much it has risen this year.

texts: Oil, week by week
May 2019: you put **€1,000** into WTI oil, just before a pandemic and a war. Live through it with **real data** and decide whether to sell.
April 2020: the world is in lockdown. How low does your €1,000 go?
About €900: the world always needs oil
About €600
Less than €350
The week of 20 April 2020 closed at $16.94 a barrel: **−68 %**. Your €1,000 was worth about €317.
Make it to the end, whether you sell or not.
From −68 % in 2020 to more than double in 2022: crude moves on **supply, demand and geopolitics**, and it does so violently.
You've sold. See what happens next…
Empty roads and almost nowhere left to store crude. Do you sell?
Crude is soaring! Not long ago nobody wanted it.
Hit «Start». You can sell whenever you like
What moves crude?
The price of oil depends on how much is wanted, how much is produced and how much is left over. What does it usually do in each case?
Tends to rise
Tends to fall
OPEC+ cuts production
Less supply with the same demand: the price goes up.
Global recession
Less gets made and people travel less: demand falls.
Conflict in the Strait of Hormuz
It rises on fears that supply will be cut off.
Full inventories and nowhere left to store it
Too much crude: downward pressure, like in April 2020.
China grows faster than expected
The US and China carry the most weight in demand.
Global lockdown: nobody travels
What happened in 2020: demand collapsed overnight.
Sort the six cases.
**OPEC+** (OPEC, founded in 1960, plus Russia and others since 2016) agrees how much gets produced; demand is driven mainly by the US and China.
Hint: is there more crude than people want, or less?
Nice! Supply, demand, storage and geopolitics.
Does crude rise or fall? Sort each case

steps.title: Brent, WTI and three shocks
steps.body:
**Brent** (North Sea) is the benchmark in Europe; **WTI** (Texas, delivered at Cushing), in the US. They're priced in **dollars per barrel** (about 159 litres): that's why the dollar matters for Spain too.

• **1973:** the OPEC embargo quadrupled the price.
• **2008:** WTI came close to **$147** in July… and by December it was below $40.
• **20 April 2020:** the May WTI contract closed at **−$37.63**: sellers were paying to have it taken off their hands.
steps.key: Oil moves on supply, demand and geopolitics, and it can do so violently.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, compare the WTI oil chart with the Brent one.

texts: Irene's chocolate
Irene
I run a chocolate shop and my supplier has put the price up again. It's madness!
2024: poor cocoa harvests in West Africa.
What do you think happened to cocoa that year?
It went up a bit, like inflation
Much more: cocoa rose **178 %** in 2024.
It soared: smaller harvest, much higher price
That's it! It rose **178 %** in a year: it almost tripled.
It fell, because less chocolate was being sold
The other way round: with a smaller harvest, cocoa rose **178 %**.
In 2022, the invasion of Ukraine drove wheat to 14-year highs.
Russia and Ukraine made up about 30 % of world exports.
What if I invest in cocoa to make up for it?
It's traded through futures: it's not as simple as «buying cocoa».
Economy or weather?
Some commodities move with the **economy** and others with the **fields**. Which type is each one?
Metal: driven by the economy
Agricultural: driven by the weather
Copper
Cables, construction, electric cars: it's in almost everything that gets made.
Coffee
A frost or a drought in Brazil is enough to send it soaring.
Lithium
It goes into batteries: it depends on industry.
Wheat
Harvests, weather and wars in the big exporting countries.
Aluminium
An industrial metal: it rises and falls with what gets made.
Cocoa
It depends on harvests in West Africa.
Sort the six commodities.
Copper is nicknamed **«Dr Copper»** because its price tends to anticipate how the economy is doing. Agricultural commodities depend on **harvests, weather and wars**.
Hint: does it come from a mine or a field?
Nice! Each commodity has its own driver.
Metal or agricultural? Sort each one

steps.title: Much more volatile
steps.body:
**Silver** is half jewellery, half industry: almost **60 %** of its demand in 2024 was industrial (electronics, solar panels). Aluminium, nickel and lithium depend on industry and batteries.

Agricultural commodities can double or crash because of a drought or a frost. They're also traded through **futures**, so investing in them isn't as simple as «buying coffee».
steps.key: Industrial metals: a thermometer for the economy. Agricultural commodities: weather and harvests.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for copper and add it to Favourites as an economic thermometer.

texts: Dani's mining company
Dani
Gold is up 10 % and my mining stock is up much more. How can that be?
The miner digs out each ounce at a cost of $1,500 and sells it for $2,000.
If gold rises 10 %, how much does the margin per ounce rise?
10 %, like gold
The cost doesn't rise: the margin goes from $500 to $700, **+40 %**.
That's it! Fixed costs **amplify** whatever the metal does.
Not at all: the margin is fixed
The cost is fixed, the margin isn't: it goes from $500 to $700.
So miners are better than gold!
And the other way round: if gold falls 10 %, the margin falls 40 %.
Direct or through a company?
There are four routes: **physical** metal, **ETCs** (traded like an ETF), **futures** and **shares** in mining or oil companies. Which one gives you the price directly?
Direct exposure to the price
Through a company
Gold bars and coins
You own the metal, but you have to store it and you pay a margin when you buy and sell.
Shares in a gold miner
They depend on gold, but also on the company's costs, debt and management.
Physical gold ETC
It trades on the stock market and is backed by gold bars kept in a vault.
Shares in an oil company
It pays dividends; a barrel doesn't. It's a different business.
WTI future
A contract to buy or sell on a set date: leveraged and complex.
Shares in a copper miner
You're buying the company, with its management, its costs and its debt.
Sort the six ways to invest.
With a company you're also buying its **management, debt and costs**: investing in gold isn't the same as investing in a gold miner.
Hint: are you buying the commodity or a business?
Nice! Each route has very different risks.
Direct or through a company?
Gold, or those who dig it up
Real data from 2007 to 2025: you have **€10,000** in gold. Move it into shares of **gold mining companies** and compare.
Gold
Gold mining companies
If gold multiplied sixfold over those years, what did gold miners do?
They gained even more
They gained less than half as much and fell much further along the way
The same as gold
Gold ended at **€61,131**; the miners, at **€25,451**. And at their worst the miners were down 77 %, against 43 % for gold.
Move everything to miners and look at the worst fall.
A mining company is a **business**: it has costs, debt and managers. Its share price depends on gold, but also on all of that. **Investing in gold isn't the same as investing in a gold miner.**
A 77 % fall: to recover from it you have to multiply by more than four.
Move the weight between gold and the miners

steps.title: Before you buy
steps.body:
• **Physical:** you own the metal, but you have to store it and you pay a margin when you buy and sell.
• **ETC:** traded like an ETF; technically it's a debt security. Gold ETCs are usually backed by physical metal; oil or agricultural ones use **futures**, with a hidden cost you'll see in the next lesson.

In Spain, ETCs are not funds: you can't switch between them without paying tax, and the tax office treats their result differently from an ETF's. Read the key information document and check whether the product is **physical** or tracks with **futures**.
steps.key: Investing in gold isn't the same as investing in a gold miner.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, compare the gold chart with that of the GDX miners ETF.

texts: The fund that lost money while crude stood still
Leo
I bought an oil fund. The barrel price hasn't moved… and I'm losing money. Why?
A fund doesn't want barrels delivered: before the contract expires, it sells the near one and buys the next.
Leo's fund has $1,000 in the May future, at $20. When it rolls over, it buys the June one, at $25.
How many barrels does the fund control now?
The same 50
With $1,000 at $25 it only buys **40 barrels**, not 50.
That's it! In contango, each roll-over leaves you with fewer barrels.
More than 50
That would happen in backwardation, with the next one cheaper.
If June expires at $20, the fund is worth 40 × $20 = $800: **−20 %**.
And crude hasn't even moved. That's the **cost of contango**.
The futures curve
A future locks in today the price of a barrel delivered later, and each month has its own price. If the later one is **more expensive**, it's **contango**; if it's **cheaper**, **backwardation**.
Contango
Backwardation
June at $25 and July at $28
Later months dearer than nearer ones: contango.
June at $90 and July at $85
Later months cheaper: backwardation.
There's too much crude and storing it costs money
Whoever stores it charges that cost in the later futures.
There's a shortage: everyone wants it now
Today's barrel is worth more than tomorrow's.
When you roll over, the same money buys fewer barrels
You sell the near one cheap and buy the next one dear.
When you roll over, the same money buys more barrels
You sell the near one dear and buy the next one cheap.
Sort the six cases.
**In contango, rolling over costs you**: with the same money, you have fewer barrels each month. In backwardation it's the other way round: rolling over adds.
Hint: is the later month dearer or cheaper?
Nice! That's exactly what happened to Leo's fund.
Contango or backwardation? Sort each case

steps.title: The 2020 case
steps.body:
In April 2020 there was so much spare crude that the May WTI contract hit **−$37.63**, while the following ones were worth much more. The biggest US oil ETF (USO) **lost around 68 % in 2020**, while spot WTI fell around **20 %**.

And after a 68 % fall, it takes a rise of more than 200 % to get back to where you started.
steps.key: In contango, a futures fund can lose money even if crude goes up.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, compare the charts of the USO ETF and WTI oil.

u15l1-1.prompt: Look at gold from 2018 to summer 2020. What trend do you see? (Gold · weekly closes · up to the week of 03/08/2020)
u15l1-1.explanation: From about $1,200 to over $2,000: fear, low rates and the pandemic pushed money into the safe haven.

u15l1-2.prompt: Tap gold's lowest point in this period. (Gold · weekly closes · up to the week of 03/08/2020)
u15l1-2.explanation: The low came at the end of 2018, at around $1,190. From there it rose around 70 % until August 2020.

u15l1-4.prompt: What does gold generate for its owner each year?
options: Nothing: no interest and no dividends
u15l1-4.explanation: You only make money if someone pays more tomorrow. That's why you can't value it with a P/E ratio.

u15l1-6.prompt: Real chart of a commodity: 30 sessions with no name or date. What did it do over the next 10?
u15l1-6.explanation: Being a "safe haven" doesn't make an asset predictable in the short term: it has very volatile weeks too.

u15l1-7.prompt: What tends to favour gold? Select all that apply.
options: Very high and rising real rates
u15l1-7.explanation: With high real rates, a bond that pays something has the edge over an asset that pays nothing.

u15l1-11.prompt: You've bought gold at the last price. Even though it's a safe haven, place the stop a little below the last low.
u15l1-11.explanation: A safe haven falls too: gold lost as much as 42% from its 2011 peak. The stop goes a little below the last low, with some room, because if it loses it your idea is no longer valid. Sticking it right on the price is tempting, but a normal swing will trigger it.

u15l2-2.prompt: Tap the lowest point in this period (weekly closes). (WTI oil · weekly closes · up to the week of 20/04/2020)
u15l2-2.explanation: The week of 20 April 2020 closed at about $17. The −$37.63 doesn't show up in weekly closes: it was a single day and a single contract, the May one, just before it expired.

u15l2-4.prompt: March 2022: war breaks out in Ukraine and Brent soars. Pablo wants to buy oil company shares right now "because this can only go up". What do you tell him?
options: To sell everything he has in the stock market
To buy as much as he can
That the price already reflects the news and can turn quickly: he shouldn't decide based on headlines
u15l2-4.explanation: Commodities react very fast to geopolitics: by the time you read the headline, the price has already jumped.
feedback: One piece of news doesn't justify dismantling a whole portfolio.
Buying right at the peak out of euphoria is very risky: crude falls violently too (2008).
Good: after the March 2022 peak, crude fell sharply over the following months.

options: OPEC plus other producers such as Russia, who agree production quotas
u15l2-5.explanation: Since 2016 it has coordinated production across around twenty countries.

u15l2-6.prompt: Match each event with its usual effect on crude.
options: Inventories full and nowhere to store
right: Rises on fears of a supply cut

u15l2-10.prompt: Why does a strong euro make oil cheaper for Spain?
options: Because crude is paid for in dollars
Because Spain produces a lot of oil
u15l2-10.explanation: With more dollars per euro, the same barrel costs fewer euros.

u15l2-11.prompt: You've bought WTI oil at the last price. Crude moves violently: place the stop a little below the last low.
u15l2-11.explanation: With such a jumpy asset, the stop needs room: a little below the last low, where your idea stops being valid. Stuck to the price, any OPEC+ headline will trigger it; without a stop, a fall like 2020's catches you in full.

u15l3-1.prompt: Match each commodity with what moves it most.
u15l3-1.explanation: Each commodity has its own main driver.
right: Harvests and conflicts in big exporters

u15l3-4.prompt: Real chart of a metal (30 sessions, no name or date). What did it do over the next 10?
u15l3-4.explanation: Metals used both in industry and as investments are pushed by two forces at once, the economy and fear. That makes them very volatile.

u15l3-5.prompt: Another real metal, another 30 sessions. Up or down?
u15l3-5.explanation: A strong move one way doesn't tell you about the next: some metals move 10 % in a few weeks, in either direction.

u15l3-8.prompt: A frost in Brazil threatens the coffee harvest. Marta runs a café in Valencia. What's most likely?
options: Coffee beans get more expensive and her costs go up
It won't affect her because she buys from a Spanish supplier
u15l3-8.explanation: With agricultural commodities, the weather in a big producer moves the global price.
feedback: That's it: less supply, higher price. In 2024 drought in Brazil pushed arabica to record highs.
A bad harvest reduces supply: normally the opposite happens.
Brazil is the world's biggest producer: the global price ends up reaching her supplier.

u15l3-10.prompt: What can push up the price of an agricultural commodity? Select all that apply.
options: A drought in a big producer
u15l3-10.explanation: A record harvest increases supply and usually lowers the price.

u15l4-1.prompt: Match each way of investing with its feature.
u15l4-1.explanation: Four routes with very different risks.
right: A contract with an expiry date and leverage
Depend on the metal and on how the company is run
Trades on an exchange and is backed by metal
You own the metal, but you have to store it

options: A listed product that tracks a commodity
u15l4-2.explanation: It trades on an exchange like an ETF, but tracks a commodity.

u15l4-6.prompt: Physical gold ETCs usually have bars stored in a vault to back the product.
u15l4-6.explanation: That's why they track gold very closely, minus their small annual fee.

u15l4-7.prompt: Bruno wants to "invest in oil". He wants to understand properly what he's buying and not use leverage. Which option does he rule out first?
options: Leveraged WTI futures from an app
u15l4-7.explanation: Leveraged futures aren't for beginners: you can lose money very fast.
feedback: It's the easiest to understand, although it doesn't track the barrel exactly.
It's not the first one to rule out, but it has futures roll costs: he needs to understand them first.
That's it: leverage and expiry dates are exactly what he wants to avoid.

u15l4-9.prompt: What are the drawbacks of gold bars? Select all that apply.
options: The gap between buying and selling price can be large
You have to store and insure it
u15l4-9.explanation: Gold pays nothing; and buying and selling it physically has costs.

u15l4-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: That's CFDs or leveraged futures: a 10 % move against you wipes out everything, and promising profits is a bad sign
u15l4-10.explanation: At 1:10, a 10 % move against you takes you to zero. CFDs are complex instruments and come with a high risk of losing money rapidly due to leverage. Between 74 and 89 % of retail investor accounts lose money when trading CFDs.
feedback: OK, I'd better understand what an ETC is before touching anything leveraged.
At 1:10, a 10 % move against you wipes out everything. And promising 300 % is a red flag.
lines: I saw an ad: "Trade oil at 1:10 and make 300 % this month" 🛢️

u15l5-4.prompt: Tap WTI's highest point in this period (weekly closes). (WTI oil · weekly closes · up to the week of 20/04/2020)
u15l5-4.explanation: About $63 in January 2020. Three months later it was closing weeks below $20, and the May contract even traded in negative territory.

u15l5-5.prompt: Real oil chart: 30 sessions with no date. What did crude do over the next 10?
u15l5-5.explanation: Even if you got the direction of the barrel right, a futures fund in contango could make quite a bit less, or even lose money.

u15l5-6.prompt: An oil futures fund always tracks the barrel price you see in the news exactly.
u15l5-6.explanation: The one in the news is the near contract; the fund rolls contracts and pays (or earns) the difference along the curve.

u15l5-7.prompt: Match each term with its definition.
u15l5-7.explanation: With these four words you already understand why an oil fund doesn't track the barrel.
right: Selling the near contract and buying the next one
Later futures cost less than nearer ones
Later futures cost more than nearer ones

u15l5-8.prompt: April 2020. Ana sees crude on the floor and buys an oil futures fund "for when it recovers". What risk hasn't she looked at?
options: The cost of rolling futures in contango
None: if crude rises, she makes the same
The fund being priced in dollars
u15l5-8.explanation: With commodities, the product matters as much as the direction of the price.
feedback: Exactly: in 2020 USO lost about 68 % while spot WTI fell around 20 %.
With such steep contango, every roll costs her barrels: even if crude recovers, the fund can be left far behind.
It's a risk, but a small one compared with the contango at that time.

u15l5-11.prompt: Laura wants to track the price of gold for years without paying the cost of rolling futures. Which product does she look at first?
options: A gold futures fund that rolls its contracts every month
A physical gold ETC, backed by bars
u15l5-11.explanation: The right one works because a physical product doesn't have to roll contracts, so contango doesn't affect it. The futures fund looks the same, but it can fall far behind the metal.
feedback: It's precisely the one that pays for rolling: in contango, every contract change subtracts.
It adds leverage and the costs of holding the position: it isn't meant to be held for years.
Good: it doesn't roll futures, because it holds the metal. It tracks gold closely, minus its annual fee.
